we need to be more ambitious in our thinking.
The UK is currently in a race with other countries to capture the potential economic benefits of the emerging blue economy, which is estimated to reach £280bn a year by 2050.
This presents a fantastic opportunity for Wales.
The Government’s Industrial Strategy White Paper has recognised that the UK is lagging behind our international competitors, such as China, in the development and adoption of blue economy technologies.
A report by the International Chamber of Shipping in 2017 also highlighted the need for the UK to develop a blue economy strategy. It pointed out that in 2015, the UK’s blue economy accounted for 1.4% of GDP. By comparison, China’s accounted for 5.3% of GDP, and Norway’s for 4.8%.
In terms of the development of blue economy technologies, China has been investing in this area for over a decade and is the global leader in the manufacture of renewable energy technologies. Other countries, such as Australia and the US, are also investing heavily in this sector.
The Government has to recognise that the UK is currently falling behind on the development and adoption of these technologies. The Government needs to take a proactive approach and develop a blue economy strategy for the UK, rather than waiting for others to lead the way.
The UK needs to take advantage of its unique position at the heart of the world’s busiest shipping lanes and to establish itself as the global hub for the development and manufacture of blue economy technologies.
This will require investment in research and development and the creation of a supportive regulatory and commercial environment.
The UK Government has already taken steps in this direction by establishing the Offshore Wind Sector Deal in 2017, which aims to drive innovation and reduce the cost of offshore wind energy.
This is a good start, but the Government needs to go further and take a more proactive approach to the development of the blue economy.

The Bill recognises the fundamental human right to water by establishing a statutory right to water for all people resident in the State. It seeks to ensure that people in this State have access to water that is safe and clean. The Bill will also give water service providers a clear obligation to ensure that their actions do not interfere with the human right to water and, where they do, to take steps to remedy that interference.
As the Bill is a private Members’ Bill, the Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government is not in a position to outline what the Department would propose to do in the event the Bill is enacted. However, given the Bill’s importance, it is worth considering some of the key provisions and how they may operate.
I will begin with the provision of a universal right to water, which is at the heart of the Bill. The Bill defines water as “an essential human need and a public good, which has an essential role in the realisation of human rights, health, dignity and well-being.” The Bill establishes that everyone in the State has a right to an amount of water that is sufficient to meet their basic needs. In this regard, the Bill provides for a level of water services that is affordable, sufficient, safe, acceptable, physically accessible, socially accessible and culturally appropriate.
The Bill’s provision of a right to water follows the example of countries such as South Africa, Ecuador and Bolivia. It is also based on the principles of the United Nations Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights’ General Comment No. 15. The Committee has outlined the right to water as a basic human right, as a fundamental component of living with dignity, and as essential for the realisation of other human rights. The Committee’s General Comment No. 15 provides a detailed framework for the realisation of the human right to water, which the Bill seeks to implement.

Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981, which protects birds by prohibiting the deliberate killing, injuring or taking of wild birds, or the deliberate destruction of their nests, eggs or habitats. The main change that the Bill would make is to increase the maximum fine from £5,000 to £20,000. I will also ask the House to agree to a small amendment that would replace a £5,000 fine with an £18,000 fine in the offence of possessing, controlling or selling wild birds in a manner that involves cruelty to the birds.
The Bill would also introduce a number of measures to help enforce the law. In particular, it would give the police, the Environment Agency and the RSPCA powers to apply to a court for the forfeiture of items that are used in the commission of offences under section 26, or for the forfeiture of profits gained from committing such offences. The measures are aimed at tackling the commercial exploitation of birds and preventing those who commit these offences from making money from them. They would allow the authorities to take away the tools of the trade, such as guns and traps, and prevent people from benefiting financially from their crimes.
I should also say that it was not my intention to amend the offence of injuring wild birds. Although the penalties for taking wild birds are being increased, the penalties for injuring birds are not being increased. Some people may wonder why the penalties for injuring wild birds are not being increased. The reason is that the maximum fine for injury offences is currently £5,000. The Government have recently increased the penalties for the same offence for injury of other wild animals to £20,000, and we do not want to create a situation in which those who injure wild birds are treated more leniently than those who injure other wild animals. I will return to the question of injury and the protection of wild birds later in my remarks.

The Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) of the United Nations estimated in 2011 that we waste a third of the food that is produced, which translates into approximately 1.3 billion tonnes. We could feed 2 billion people every year with the food that is wasted. The Food Standards Agency estimates that the average household in the UK throws away £680 worth of food and drink each year, which is equivalent to 70 kg of food waste per person annually.
According to the United Nations Environment Programme, approximately 3.3 gigatonnes of food is wasted every year. Of that, 30% could be saved by reducing the browning and spoiling of fruit and vegetables. At the same time, the world population is expected to increase by 2 billion people by 2050, and the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation estimates that we need to increase food production by 70% to meet their needs.
The FAO has identified the reduction of food waste as one of the most effective ways of ensuring a sustainable food supply to meet the demands of the world’s growing population. If we can reduce the amount of food we waste, it is a good way of ensuring that we have enough food to meet the needs of an increased population.
The reduction of food waste is one of the key priorities of the food strategy that is being developed by my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State. It is one of the seven commitments that she set out last week. The Government are working closely with the food industry and have already invested more than £200 million in reducing food waste through the waste and resource action programme. The food industry is already looking to develop new technologies and innovative solutions to reduce waste and spoilage.

The teller asked my mother to sign the account as a guarantor, which she did. I was given a passbook and I used to get a free copy of the Financial Times every day. I would go into town and have breakfast at the YMCA and read the paper over my eggs and bacon and my cup of tea.
I never went into overdraft or overdraw my account. I would get a statement every month and keep it in a folder. The money I earned from my Saturday job would be paid into the account. The bank was a safe place to keep my money and my mother, who was a widow, was happy that I had a bank account.
I never had an overdraft account with the bank and never needed one. If I wanted to buy something I would save up for it and then buy it. I had a bicycle and then a car, both bought with money I had saved up.
But that was then, and now things are very different. The current generation of young people do not have the same attitudes. They are more inclined to use their credit card to make purchases and then pay off the credit card at the end of the month. The credit card company, of course, charges a high rate of interest on the unpaid balance, but I think this is regarded as a convenience fee and not as a form of usury. In any event, many young people pay off their credit card in full at the end of the month.
The new generation of young people have a different attitude to money. They have no need for a bank account and are quite happy to use their credit card for most purchases. This is a far cry from my day when the bank was a safe place to keep your money and a passbook was a record of your transactions.

This Government could do a great deal to alleviate the pain for pensioners and others by making the most of the energy we already have. The UK has some of the most favourable conditions for solar and wind power in Europe. Harnessing this could cut our reliance on expensive imported gas, and free up money for pensioners.
The government has set a target to generate 70% of the UK’s electricity from renewable sources by 2030. But the current administration has failed to implement the policies necessary to achieve it.
Instead, it has taken us backwards, scrapping many of the schemes introduced by the previous government to help people generate their own power and pay less for their energy. While the UK has great renewable energy potential, the government has failed to act.
This is why I have called on the Prime Minister to introduce a new £10 billion solar subsidy scheme for the UK.
This scheme would incentivise the installation of solar panels on homes and businesses, and help kickstart the solar industry in the UK, which has suffered since the last government’s cuts. It would provide an immediate boost to the economy, supporting local jobs and reducing our reliance on gas imports.
The cost would be worth it. If we achieve the government’s own target of 70% renewable energy by 2030, the UK could save £140bn on energy bills by 2050. The subsidies needed to achieve this target would be a fraction of this amount.
The UK has an opportunity to create a cleaner, greener future. But we must act now.
This is not a partisan issue. It is about putting the country first, cutting energy costs and helping pensioners.
I urge the Prime Minister to take the lead and introduce a new solar subsidy scheme that will benefit us all.

The Minister’s last minute announcement of the budget last night has left many people wondering if she’s playing a game of musical chairs with budget cuts. A cut in the cost of a pint of beer is good news but it is hardly a solution for the problems we face. A cut of €2.1 million in the cost of the Dáil is nothing compared to the hundreds of millions of euro cut in public services. The Minister’s announcement of an extra €20 million in the budget to pay the Irish Sports Council is more money thrown into the hole. We are on the verge of a health crisis and the budget is being used to pay for the Irish Sports Council. The Minister’s new sports development fund is a way to avoid cutting the budget of the Department of Education by €100 million. This is an absolute disgrace. And of course the reign of Edward VIII was not merely a significant moment in British political and constitutional history. It was also a significant moment in British social and cultural history. This should also be the case for fiscal policy, which deals with the government’s budget, tax, and spending decisions.
The U.S. federal government is facing a growing deficit and high national debt. In the last few years, a majority of economists have agreed that the most pressing concern for U.S. fiscal policy is the national debt. The debt is the total of all spending the government has done that is not funded by tax revenue. The debt has increased over the last decade because of a variety of factors. The most significant of these is the 2007–2008 recession. The recession caused a significant drop in tax revenue because economic activity decreased and people were not earning as much money. At the same time, the government increased spending in order to stimulate the economy. A majority of economists feel that the stimulus spending was necessary and helped the economy recover more quickly.
In 2009, the government instituted a 10 percent payroll tax holiday, in which the government temporarily removed 10 percent of the Social Security tax paid by workers. The tax holiday was intended to increase workers’ take-home pay and spur economic activity. The tax holiday is an example of expansionary fiscal policy. It is expansionary because it increased the amount of money workers had to spend. Expansionary fiscal policy is used to encourage economic activity when the economy is slow.
Expansionary fiscal policy is also used when the government borrows money and spends it on new programs or projects. The idea is that the government’s spending will increase economic activity and stimulate growth. When the government borrows money, it adds to the national debt.

The theme for this year’s commemoration is “be the light in the darkness”. It is a fitting message, and one which I feel is particularly important in the context of the events we are marking.
It is, sadly, true that in the 70 years since the Holocaust, we have witnessed countless other examples of mass violence, and in many cases have failed to act to prevent or stop them.
We will never be able to change the past, but we can and must learn from the mistakes we have made.
The people who suffered as a result of the Holocaust did not stop being human – or being individuals – when they were dehumanised in the concentration camps.
Their humanity was always there, hidden but not extinguished – and it was these small acts of kindness and humanity that helped so many of them survive.
I hope the work of the Holocaust Memorial Day Trust, and the events we have marked today, can act as a beacon of hope and a light in the darkness.
I am confident that by continuing to work together, and to tell the stories of the past, we can create a better future.
And that, in the end, will be our greatest tribute to those who were lost.

There is a potential solution to this problem. Another problem has arisen with the introduction of the UK Ancestry visa route, which was introduced to allow Commonwealth nationals to come and work in the UK. The fact that the referendum result was a decision on an issue of national importance was widely acknowledged. When the pipeline was built in the 1950s, it was constructed in a time of low oil prices, which meant that the pipeline was built to carry only 300,000 barrels per day. Alberta was facing a pricing crisis, and the federal and provincial governments needed to act. In 2013, the NDP-NDP government of Alberta purchased the pipeline from Kinder Morgan, with the intention of building a twin pipeline to carry 590,000 barrels per day from the oil sands to the west coast. In 2014, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Premier Rachel Notley came together to announce the Alberta government's purchase of the pipeline, and the plan for the expansion to take place. They stated that the expansion would be built by a private sector company, which would be contracted to do the expansion work. The pipeline and expansion would be financed through revenue from oil and gas royalties, which would then be reinvested in public services, infrastructure, and the economy.

How is the fire extinguished?
The problem with lithium-ion battery fires is that they are difficult to put out, and the heat can be very intense. A dry chemical fire extinguisher can be used, but the flames will return after the extinguishing agent has been applied. The only effective way to put out the fire is to cool the cells to a safe temperature. This requires large amounts of water.
What kind of damage does a fire cause?
A fire can damage everything around it. In addition to causing damage to the structure, it can also cause injuries or even death, both directly from the fire itself and from the toxic gases released by the fire.
How do you protect yourself against a fire?
The best way to protect yourself against a fire is to prevent it from happening in the first place. This can be done by storing the batteries in a safe location, away from heat sources and flammable materials. You should also make sure that the batteries are properly maintained and replaced if they are damaged or show signs of wear.
What do you do if a fire starts?
If a fire starts, you should evacuate the area immediately and call the fire department. Do not attempt to extinguish the fire yourself, as this can be dangerous. If the fire is small and contained, you can use a dry chemical fire extinguisher to try to put it out. However, if the fire is large or spreading, you should evacuate the area and let the fire department handle it.
What are the consequences of a fire?
The consequences of a fire can be severe. A fire can cause damage to the structure, injury or death, and environmental damage. Fires can also cause economic damage, as they can disrupt business and cause property damage.

(NAO) estimates that 400,000 children have no child maintenance payments.
The NAO have concluded that the DWP’s Child Maintenance Service (CMS) has been ineffective in helping parents to make and follow agreements to support their children, and has failed to protect the most vulnerable children.
Since April 2012 the CMS has been responsible for managing child maintenance arrangements between separated parents in England and Wales. It is funded by the government and was introduced in order to remove the need for parents to go to court in order to agree a child maintenance arrangement.
The NAO found that the DWP’s CMS has not achieved its aim to support children by helping parents to make and follow child maintenance arrangements. This has been due to the service failing to address issues with the complexity and inflexibility of its system, not improving the information it collects and shares, and not ensuring that all parents have a child maintenance arrangement in place.
As of the end of June 2022, approximately 400,000 children had no child maintenance payments, and £493.5 million of arrears had accumulated from children who did have an arrangement. These arrears include £271 million from those who had been unable to agree a payment for more than 12 months, and an estimated £39 million that were over three years old.
The NAO concluded that the CMS had not improved its performance over time, and that the DWP’s targets for increasing payments to children were not robust and were not met. The NAO also found that the DWP’s 2018 performance review of the CMS did not lead to significant improvements being made, and that the service was not performing well when the review took place.

The Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992, which I believe is still in force, is the current framework for dealing with the rights and obligations of trade unions and employers. The 1992 act provides a balance between the right of trade unions to engage in industrial disputes and the right of employers to run their businesses without industrial disruption. I do not think that either side can be said to be over-protected by that legislation. In fact, the balance of protection is towards employers.
The 1992 act gives trade unions the right to take strike action in pursuit of their members’ interests. It also provides that trade union funds may be used to finance or subsidise strikes, provided that they are for a “trade dispute”. However, the legislation imposes obligations on trade unions. For example, the union must consult its members and hold a ballot of them before deciding to take strike action. A majority of members must vote for the strike, and the ballot must be supervised by an independent official from the certification officer. If a union does not comply with those provisions, the strike is not legal.
It is important to remember that the purpose of the provisions is to ensure that a legal strike is not a surprise to either employers or the public, and that a majority of union members want the action. It is not to protect the unions from the consequences of their actions. Once a legal strike has been held, the union is liable for any loss or damage that it causes to an employer. That is because the law says that it is unlawful to picket or strike in pursuit of a trade dispute. The unions must therefore be liable for their actions.

The oil and gas industry is in the midst of a transformation, as the world transitions to a low-carbon future. Canadian gas has a role to play in this future. In 2020, the International Energy Agency (IEA) stated that, by 2030, more than 80% of Canada's natural gas demand must come from non-fossil sources to reach its climate objectives.

In the coming years, energy markets will be reshaped by the transition to low-carbon, with significant implications for Canadian gas producers. To help Canada meet its emission reduction commitments, the industry has been focused on reducing its emissions and increasing the share of low-carbon gas, such as biogas and RNG, in the overall gas mix.

Canadian gas producers are well-positioned to provide this low-carbon gas and are committed to helping the world reach its climate objectives. To achieve this, gas producers are working to reduce their emissions and increase the share of low-carbon gas in the overall gas mix.

What are the benefits of RNG?

RNG is a type of biogas produced from organic waste such as food waste, agricultural waste, and sewage sludge. It can be used in the same way as natural gas, and can be used to generate electricity, heat, and transportation fuels. It is an attractive option for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, as it can be produced from waste that would otherwise be released into the atmosphere. Additionally, RNG can be used in existing natural gas infrastructure, making it a cost-effective solution for reducing emissions.

Well, it’s time for another post on the intersection between public health and education, and I thought we’d look at the question of what a school can and cannot do in terms of excluding children from school for reasons of ill health. This is a big issue right now, as the debate continues about the exclusion of children with measles and who are unvaccinated.
The short answer is that schools have a duty to protect other children from infection, but they also have a duty to protect individual children’s rights to education. It is a balancing act.
In my state of Western Australia, the relevant legislation is the Education Act 1984. It is the Education Act that mandates compulsory education, and it is the Education Act that gives the government the power to enforce it, through fines or even imprisonment (though this is a very last resort). It is also the Act that gives the government power to set the conditions for the operation of schools, and this is where the health issues arise.
In the Education Act, there are only three grounds on which a child can be excluded from school:
- They are absent for a reason other than illness or injury, and they fail to return to school within five days of the reason for their absence ceasing; or
- They are absent for illness or injury, and they fail to return to school within 30 days of the last day of absence; or
- They have a communicable disease.
In the case of the latter, the school must be satisfied that the disease is communicable. But what does that mean? In WA, the definition of ‘communicable disease’ is set out in the Public Health Act 2016. This Act defines communicable disease as “disease that is, or might be, capable of being transmitted from one person to another person.”

The Bill provides the Government with the authority to enter into contracts on behalf of EirGrid to procure backup electricity generation capacity. This means that we can provide the necessary financial and regulatory certainty to incentivise private companies to invest in this capacity.
The Government has been in discussions with the European Commission for some time in respect of the proposed contracts for difference, which are an element of the wider electricity market reform package.
The contracts for difference are a mechanism designed to encourage investment in low carbon electricity generation. A contract for difference works by setting a strike price (the price at which the generator will sell electricity). If the market price is below the strike price, the generator will be paid the difference between the two prices. Conversely, if the market price is above the strike price, the generator will be required to pay the difference to the buyer.
The contracts for difference are intended to be a temporary measure to encourage new investments in low carbon electricity generation, but the European Commission has not yet formally approved them.
The Bill will give the Government the power to enter into contracts for difference without the need to refer each contract to the European Commission. This is an administrative measure which will not change any of the terms of the contracts.
If the European Commission were to raise concerns about a contract that was entered into under this Bill, the Government would be able to refer the contract to the Commission. However, the Bill does not provide a mechanism to refer contracts back to the Commission.
The Bill also provides the Government with the power to enter into contracts for capacity on behalf of EirGrid. A contract for capacity is a mechanism designed to ensure that there is enough generation capacity to meet demand at all times. It works by requiring generators to commit to having a certain amount of capacity available at all times. If they fail to do so, they will be required to pay a penalty. Conversely, if they are able to meet their commitments, they will be paid a capacity payment.

The judgment has also raised the question as to whether US firms should start relying on alternative transfer mechanisms such as Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) to transfer data from the EU to the US. BCRs allow multinational companies to make internal transfers of personal data between their EU and non-EU affiliates (which can include the US) without the need for any additional transfer mechanism. BCRs can also be used to transfer personal data from the EU to the US on behalf of other companies.
BCRs are not as simple to implement as the SCCs and are often a long-term solution to data protection challenges. For these reasons, they may be a more complex alternative for some US firms.
How can US firms prepare for the Schrems II judgment?
The Schrems II judgment has certainly had a significant impact on the way in which US firms conduct business. It has forced a number of companies to review their data transfer practices, with many realising that they may need to make changes to their policies and procedures to ensure compliance with the GDPR.
For this reason, US firms should consider:
Reviewing existing agreements to ensure that the SCCs are still valid;
Considering other legal means of transferring data; and
Reviewing data protection policies and procedures.

The COVID-19 pandemic has brought to light many of the deep social and economic inequities and vulnerabilities that our country faced before this crisis. The pandemic is not only a public health crisis but also an economic, social, and political crisis that is disproportionately impacting vulnerable Canadians.
The 2017 census showed that 24% of British Columbians over the age of 65, or 680,000 seniors, were living in poverty. The 2016 census showed that over 145,000 British Columbians, or 4.2% of the population, were living in poverty. However, the 2019 census of the Canadian Poverty Institute showed that the poverty rate in British Columbia was actually 14.3%, or 398,000 people, higher than what was previously reported. In addition, the poverty rate for children in British Columbia was 18.7%, and the poverty rate for women in B.C. was 16.9%.
The poverty rate in British Columbia is higher than the national average. This is due to the fact that British Columbia has higher housing costs and is one of the more expensive provinces to live in. The poverty rate in British Columbia has been rising and continues to do so. The federal government has failed to provide the necessary funding to support housing and affordable housing in this country. The federal government has failed to provide adequate funding to support health care in this country.
The pandemic has brought to light the fact that we have a major housing crisis in this country, and we are seeing that our homeless shelters are not safe places for people to live during this pandemic. We are seeing that our long-term care facilities are not adequately funded. As a result, we are seeing too many people die. We are seeing that our health care system is not properly funded and too many people are going without health care.

The Deputy's concerns are valid, and I will address them comprehensively. The HSE has established a robust process for evaluating and approving orphan drugs. When an orphan drug is applied for reimbursement, the HSE conducts a thorough assessment, including a health technology assessment (HTA) to evaluate the drug's clinical effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness. This process involves input from clinical experts and other stakeholders to ensure that the decision is based on sound evidence. 

Moreover, the HSE has a long-term financial planning mechanism in place. As an employer, the HSE must ensure that it can provide healthcare to the population at a reasonable cost. If a particular treatment, such as an orphan drug, is deemed too costly, the HSE will consider alternative options or negotiate with the pharmaceutical company to find a more affordable solution. The HSE also takes into account the broader economic implications, including the potential impact on future healthcare costs and the ability to fund other necessary treatments.

Additionally, the HSE has a duty to balance the needs of individual patients with the overall sustainability of the healthcare system. While it is important to provide access to life-saving treatments, the HSE must also ensure that it can continue to offer a comprehensive range of services to all patients. This is why the HSE has established a clear set of criteria for evaluating orphan drugs, including considerations of patient benefit, clinical need, and financial feasibility.

In summary, the HSE is committed to managing the costs of orphan drugs in a way that ensures both patient access and the long-term sustainability of the healthcare system. The HSE will continue to monitor the situation and make informed decisions based on the available evidence and expert advice.

We know that the cost of housing is increasing for all Canadians. Families and individuals have faced significant increases in housing costs in the last couple of years, and many are being forced to choose between other necessities and housing.
For example, a report from the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation found that between 2018 and 2020, 35% of the population had difficulty paying for their housing costs. This has only increased with the rising cost of housing and inflation.
Rising housing costs and lack of affordable housing are leading to more people experiencing homelessness. There are currently 150,000 people experiencing homelessness in Canada, including 1 in 5 who are children.
Rising housing costs are also contributing to a rise in homelessness among the Indigenous population. There are 37,000 Indigenous people experiencing homelessness, and Indigenous people are 14 times more likely than non-Indigenous people to experience homelessness.

The lack of affordable housing and the high cost of housing is hurting people’s health and well-being. In a survey of people experiencing homelessness, 89% reported that housing instability affected their mental health. In another survey of people in need of housing, 57% reported that it negatively affected their physical health.

The Life Sentence Review Board was established in 2007 under the Criminal Justice (Supervision of Certain Persons Convicted of Serious Offences) Act 2006. It may also review sentences imposed on the advice of the court or a review body established to review life sentences. It is important to note that the board is not a court and does not have the authority to change the sentence imposed by the judge. It does not have the power to impose a sentence or change a sentence. It does not have the authority to release a prisoner. Instead, its function is to review the sentence and make recommendations to the Minister for Justice and Equality.
The board is currently chaired by the President of the High Court, Mr. Justice Peter Charleton, and is comprised of members with extensive experience in the criminal justice system. The Disability Rights Commission has previously reported that people with disabilities are more likely to become unemployed and less likely to find a job when they leave school than people without disabilities. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) is not delivering the help and support that disabled people need to stay in or enter employment. This is despite disability being the biggest cause of unemployment in the UK, with 1.8 million people of working age currently unemployed.
In addition, there is not a single law to protect the rights of disabled people in the workplace, despite 2.8 million disabled people of working age wanting to work but not able to because of barriers to employment.
The Trade Union Congress (TUC) says that more than 15 million people are in insecure work, with one in four workers on zero-hours contracts. A quarter of all women and 15 per cent of all men experience pay inequality. The TUC says that this has a direct impact on disabled people, who are more likely to be in lower paid insecure jobs.
The TUC’s research shows that 24 per cent of disabled people are paid less than the National Living Wage, compared with 16 per cent of non-disabled people. The Equality and Human Rights Commission says that 40 per cent of disabled people are paid less than the living wage, and only half of disabled people are paid the living wage. The TUC says that disabled people are more likely to have to work multiple jobs and be paid less because of the discrimination they face in the labour market. In addition, the TUC says that disabled workers are three times more likely to be in precarious work arrangements, such as part-time or zero-hours contracts.
The Disability Rights Commission says that the Disability Discrimination Act 1995 is wholly inadequate for tackling the barriers to employment and participation faced by disabled people, and that there are no laws in place to protect the rights of disabled people in the workplace.

Section 49 provides for the issue of notice to vacate a residential property where a local authority believes that a person is homeless or threatened with homelessness. The Bill will ensure that tenants facing homelessness will not be subjected to a notice to vacate during the COVID-19 pandemic. Section 49 notices will be extended automatically until 30 June 2021, giving the local authority a further 30 days to determine the notice. The extension will also apply to those tenants who are in possession of a section 49 notice and are also in possession of a notice to vacate under section 22.
This measure is an important part of the Government's strategy to keep people safe in their homes, and to minimise the risk of homelessness. The automatic extension of notice periods will also have a positive impact on the work of the local authorities and housing executive by reducing the number of homelessness determinations. The Bill will also provide certainty to those landlords who are facing challenges in the current environment. Our sex offences law is in desperate need of reform. Does it follow that "A new fluidity in politics that we have never seen before is being seen."?

Yes, it does follow that "A new fluidity in politics that we have never seen before is being seen." The statement implies that the current political situation in the Parliament is experiencing a unique and unprecedented level of change and dynamism, which has not been witnessed in the past.

This new fluidity in politics can be observed in various aspects of the political landscape. One of the most prominent features is the increased volatility and uncertainty in political alliances and party affiliations. In the past, political parties and their members tended to remain loyal to their respective parties, maintaining a relatively stable and predictable political landscape. However, with the emergence of new issues, changing public opinions, and evolving political ideologies, there has been a shift towards a more dynamic and flexible political environment.

Another aspect of this new fluidity in politics is the increased prominence of individual politicians and their ability to shape political discourse and influence decision-making. The traditional structures and hierarchies that once dominated political parties have given way to a more individualistic approach, with politicians often prioritizing their personal agendas and ideologies over party lines. This has led to a more diverse and varied political landscape, where individual voices and perspectives can have a significant impact on the political process.

Additionally, the rise of new media and social networking platforms has also contributed to the new fluidity in politics. The ability to reach a wide audience and engage with people from all walks of life has given rise to new political movements and grassroots campaigns that were previously unimaginable. These platforms have allowed politicians and activists to bypass traditional gatekeepers, such as mainstream media outlets, and communicate directly with their constituents, further amplifying the dynamic nature of the political landscape.

The Government have launched the Jobs Retention Bonus, to reward employers who retain their staff and avoid compulsory redundancies in the early months of the pandemic. To be eligible for the £1,000 per employee Jobs Retention Bonus, businesses must have furloughed at least one employee and continue to employ them for at least a further six months after 31 March 2021.
The Government have also extended the Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme for the months of November and December 2020, to ensure that employers have more time to retain their employees and prepare to restart their businesses as restrictions are eased.
The Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme (CJRS) will continue to support employers in retaining staff and avoiding compulsory redundancies by allowing them to continue to place employees on furlough for any duration. This will help employers who may not have been able to keep furloughed staff on their payrolls during the summer months.
Employers will have to contribute 10% of the wage cost of their furloughed employees, with the Government covering the remaining 70%, up to a maximum of £2,187.50 per month.
All other eligibility rules will remain the same as the current scheme.
The CJRS will end at the end of December 2020, after which the Government will be in a position to review the wider economy and consider other support measures for the months ahead.

The public interest is a nebulous term which has been subject to considerable debate over many years. The Deputy is right in saying that the definition of the public interest should be expanded, but it should be expanded to a very large extent. If we are going to allow the public interest to be a determining factor in the amount of information which citizens are entitled to have, we could be left with the situation where an official decides that, in his opinion, the public interest does not demand the release of information. This is a matter for the courts, the courts of law.
The courts have interpreted what is the public interest in a wide variety of cases and have held that it is a factor to be taken into account. It is not the only factor to be taken into account. The courts have made it very clear that the public interest is a very important factor. However, that factor is balanced against the other factors and is not the only consideration. It is one of the factors which must be taken into account. It is a factor which is weighed in the scales along with the other factors. The courts have held that information must be disclosed if it is in the public interest to do so. The courts also held that if there is a likelihood that the public interest would be served by disclosure, the request must be granted. It is the public interest which must be the determining factor. This is the approach which is taken by the courts.

This approach is more accurate than the static approach taken in the 2015 Regional Waste Management Plan and the most recent local authority submissions.

What does this mean for the future?
The Supreme Court's decision in the Jordan case makes clear that the government must now do more to ensure that criminal trial delays are minimized. If the court finds that the government is unable to meet its duty to provide justice in a timely manner, the court has the power to dismiss the charges.
The government has an obligation to ensure that justice is provided in a timely manner. However, there is nothing in the government's obligations that requires it to take a specific approach to meeting this goal.
The Jordan decision does not, for example, prevent the government from establishing a special tribunal, as was done to address the 2006-2014 trial delays in the Idle No More blockades. The decision does not prevent the government from using emergency powers. However, the government's use of emergency powers must be justified by an emergency situation, not a result of the government's own failure to deliver timely justice.
Jordan, however, does prevent the government from using a legislative solution to resolve delays in the criminal justice system. For example, if the government passed legislation that delayed the commencement of the time limit on which the Jordan decision is based, it would likely be in breach of its constitutional duty to deliver timely justice.
What does this mean for Indigenous peoples?

I would like to start by paying tribute to the people of the European Union. This is not the place for a grand statement of Britain’s relationship with Europe, but rather for me to say what we expect to achieve from our departure from Europe. We are leaving the EU because we believe that the best interests of the United Kingdom are best served by it. We want a Britain that is determined to be a great trading nation, open to the world. I will not be a member of the European Union for much longer, but I will remain a friend of the European Union. What is the due diligence process and how does it impact the sale of the site?
The due diligence process is a legal obligation that buyers must undertake before making any offer on a property. It involves conducting various investigations and analyses to assess the site's condition and any potential risks or liabilities. Due diligence can include a range of activities, such as reviewing legal documents, conducting environmental assessments, and evaluating the site's physical condition. In this case, the due diligence process has revealed that the Bunratty and Craggaunowen sites have significant structural issues and require extensive repairs.
What are the potential consequences of neglecting due diligence in property transactions?
Neglecting due diligence in property transactions can have serious consequences for buyers. Failing to properly assess the condition of a site can result in unexpected costs and liabilities, such as those associated with structural repairs or environmental contamination. Buyers may also be held liable for any damages or harm caused by the site if they did not conduct due diligence. In some cases, buyers may also be required to pay for any necessary repairs or improvements before they can take possession of the property.

In the last decade, average earnings have risen 37% compared with average house price inflation of 150%. The data is provided to the relevant Member States. VMS data is an important tool for the monitoring of vessels in EU waters. The Minister for Health said he would never have got into politics if he thought the system was in such a state. I wish he had listened to his conscience then and never got into politics. In the 1960s, the Catholic Church in Ireland established a series of maternity homes for pregnant women who were unmarried. This was a time of great social and political change. The population was growing, emigration was high and the country was still reeling from the effects of partition. In many ways, this was a time of crisis and, for the Catholic Church, it was a time to act. Catholic social teaching was in its infancy and the concept of family and marriage was under threat. The Church was adamant that marriage was the only acceptable form of human relationships and, consequently, unmarried pregnant women were seen as a threat to the moral and social fabric of the country. As a result, many of these women were sent to live in maternity homes, which were run by religious orders, and were expected to give up their babies for adoption. This was a deeply traumatic experience for many women and their children.
The Church's involvement in this system was extensive. It was not just a matter of providing a place for these women to give birth, but it was also about controlling their sexuality and their reproductive choices. The Church believed that these women had sinned and that they needed to be punished for their actions. The children born in these homes were often seen as a burden, and their mothers were often ostracised by society. The Church's involvement in this system was deeply troubling and it is important that we acknowledge the harm that was done to these women and their children.

However, there are clear signals that this model of economic development is no longer fit for purpose. We are facing a new reality. We must now look to other models to support our economy, and the Government has already begun that transition.
In the past decade, we have seen a number of key challenges emerge for our economy. We have seen that the cost of doing business in Ireland has been increasing. This has been driven by many factors, including the high cost of land and labour. At the same time, we have seen an increase in the number of countries competing for multinational investment. Some have used their own state-owned assets to attract new investment, but we have not had that option available to us in the public sector. Multinationals have also been increasingly drawn to more flexible and less restrictive tax regimes. All of this has meant that we have had to respond to a more competitive environment.
Multinationals have also been facing increasing scrutiny by the EU and OECD in relation to their corporate taxation. This has resulted in a series of regulatory changes that have reduced the value of the corporate tax system in Ireland, particularly in relation to our ability to attract new investments.
We have also seen a shift in the nature of foreign direct investment (FDI) in recent years. While we have always attracted manufacturing and technology investments, we have also seen a significant increase in the number of financial services investments that have been attracted to Ireland. These investments have brought with them significant benefits to the economy, but they have also brought with them significant risks. The financial crisis of 2008 and 2009 was a stark reminder of the risks that can be associated with the financial services sector. The relief applies to first-time buyers who purchase a residential property for no more than £500,000. First-time buyers will not have to pay stamp duty on the first £300,000 of the price of the property, and they will pay stamp duty at the reduced rate of 5% on the portion of the price above £300,000. The autumn quarter figures show that the average price of a residential property purchased in the UK was £183,423. The average stamp duty land tax paid by first-time buyers was £1,913, compared to £4,125 paid by other purchasers. The relief has resulted in first-time buyers paying £2,212 less stamp duty on average. The impact of the relief on sales to first-time buyers is evident. Sales to first-time buyers rose by 27% between the spring and autumn quarters, compared to a 14% rise for all buyers. The stamp duty land tax statistics also show that sales to first-time buyers in the autumn quarter rose by 3% on the same period last year, compared to a 2% fall in sales to all buyers.

The members of the association decided to take a stand and demanded that the workday be reduced from 12 hours to eight hours. What is the legal position in respect of payment of wages, holiday pay, etc?
Workers have a common law right to be paid for work done in accordance with the terms of their contract. The Employment Rights Act 1996 introduced statutory rights as well. Under the act, workers have the right to be paid in accordance with the terms of their contract and any applicable collective agreement. They have a statutory right to be paid at least once a month (or once every two months if the payment is a holiday entitlement payment). The act also contains provisions on pay protection in respect of insolvency and also provides a statutory right for workers to be paid for paid leave and for statutory sick pay.
It is possible for workers to enter into contracts or collective agreements that allow for deferred payment. However, if employers fall into insolvency, workers are put in a very difficult position. There is no statutory obligation on employers to pay in advance in the form of a security for payment.
What are the current collective bargaining arrangements?
There is no specific legislation governing collective bargaining and it is a matter for employers and trade unions to come to agreement. However, in terms of the general law, collective bargaining and agreements must be carried out in good faith. The Employment Rights Act 1996 also provides a statutory right to be represented at disciplinary and grievance hearings. Where a trade union is recognised as being representative of a particular group of workers, it can make a claim for a trade union recognition procedure. If the trade union is found to be representative of the group of workers, the employer is obliged to enter into negotiations.
How far do collective bargaining arrangements extend in practice?
In practice, the extent to which collective bargaining arrangements extend depends on a number of factors. In some sectors of the economy, such as the public sector and the energy and transport sectors, there is a high level of collective bargaining and collective agreements

The common organisation of agricultural markets is a common EU policy that applies to all member states. It regulates the markets for agricultural products. The common organisation of agricultural markets is made up of several instruments, such as the basic regulation, the cross-compliance regulation, the organic farming regulation, the marketing standards regulation and the single payment scheme regulation. The aim is to achieve a stable market, a fair standard of living for the agricultural sector and sustainable agriculture. This is mainly achieved through various support schemes, such as the single payment scheme and the private storage aid. The single payment scheme is a scheme for direct payments from the EU to the agricultural sector, which were designed to supplement the income of farmers and thus ensure that they could continue to farm and make a living from it.
The single payment scheme is only one of several support schemes that the UK currently has in place. The main scheme is the basic payment scheme (BPS). The UK is phasing out the BPS and replacing it with the sustainable farming incentive (SFI) and the environmental land management scheme (ELMS). These schemes are not covered by this instrument.

The Bill will provide us with a new framework for the regulation of medicines, medical devices and blood components, all of which will be underpinned by a new medicines and healthcare products regulatory agency. I have had a number of opportunities to consider the Bill in detail. I have been lucky enough to visit the MHRA and look around its facilities, and I have had the opportunity to speak to the head of the agency, Sir George Alberti, and other officials. I have also met representatives of the pharmaceutical industry, the medical profession and the consumer movement. The Bill will bring about a number of very welcome changes.
The current system of regulation, based on the directive of 1965, was developed at a time when many of the problems that now confront us did not exist. We now have a far greater knowledge of what makes a medicine effective and safe, and we have had a far greater growth in the range and complexity of products that are regulated.
In 1965, the regulation of blood components was not considered necessary. Today, they are a vital part of modern medicine and blood components are widely used. The Bill will provide for their regulation for the first time. The Bill will also provide for the regulation of medical devices. Until now, there has been no regulatory framework for them.
The Bill will also bring about important changes for the regulation of medicines. The current system allows a medicine to be placed on the market if it meets a certain set of conditions, but it does not allow for the continuous monitoring of its effectiveness and safety once it is in use. The Bill will change that by introducing a regulatory regime for post-marketing studies. That will enable us to monitor the long-term effects of medicines as they are used in the real world.

What the average Canadian doesn't see is the physical and mental toll it takes on them. Often, veterans don't talk about their experiences to the public. Instead, they talk to each other. In the Veterans' Memorial Building in Edmonton, there is an organization called Soldier On. They have a variety of programs to help veterans with their physical and mental health. They also offer peer support and mentorship programs. The program that caught my attention was the one that offers art therapy.
My parents have always had an interest in art, so when I came home from my trip I thought about how I could bring the art of veterans back home. I approached Soldier On about the idea of using art as a way for veterans to tell their stories, and they were very supportive of it. After that, I put out a call for veterans to participate and was pleasantly surprised to receive over 100 submissions from across the country. The artists I selected for this exhibit, from across Canada, were all asked to submit their work with the theme of hope in mind. In the end, I selected 20 artists to participate and created a travelling exhibit that started in Edmonton and will travel to Calgary and Ottawa.
The 20 veterans' art pieces are very different from each other and represent the wide variety of experiences veterans have while serving their country. However, the common thread throughout the pieces is that the veterans found hope in their experiences. For some, this hope came from a life-changing moment in a conflict zone; for others, it was finding hope in themselves that helped them get through the difficulties they encountered. The hope that these veterans have found has helped them cope with the challenges of PTSD and other injuries they may have incurred while serving in the Canadian Forces. This exhibit is an opportunity for people to gain a better understanding of what these veterans have experienced and to see how they have been able to find hope in their lives.

What is the Canadian Armed Forces doing to promote a positive culture?
The Canadian Armed Forces has been taking steps to prevent misconduct, harassment and discrimination. As part of these efforts, the Canadian Armed Forces developed the Code of Values and Ethics, a foundational tool for members to build and develop a culture of respect and professionalism within the Canadian Armed Forces. The Code of Values and Ethics highlights the core values and ethical principles of the Canadian Armed Forces that will guide all members in their actions and behaviour.
Additionally, the Canadian Armed Forces has undertaken several initiatives to change its culture, including:
a $16.3-million investment for the Women, Peace and Security Action Plan to promote gender equality and address sexual misconduct, harassment and discrimination in the Canadian Armed Forces;
an updated harassment and discrimination policy to reduce barriers for reporting and to support those who report; and
the establishment of the Centre of Excellence for Women, Peace and Security to provide a central point of expertise to advise the Canadian Armed Forces and to help address sexual misconduct, harassment and discrimination.

What are your thoughts on the gas price cap that has been proposed?
It is important to keep the debate on the gas price cap in perspective. The European Union is not proposing a price cap; it is proposing a price cap on gas from Russia. This is not a price cap on gas in general and it is not a price cap for the entire market. The European Commission has said that its proposal for a price cap on Russian gas will not apply to any other gas suppliers.
This means that while it may be possible to cap Russian gas, it will be very difficult to cap the price of gas from other countries. The Russian government would be free to set any price it wanted, while any other gas supplier would have to set prices according to the market.
It is important to understand that we are talking about two completely different markets. The market for Russian gas is a bilateral market, meaning that it is a market that is negotiated between two parties. The market for gas from other countries is a spot market, meaning that it is a market where prices are set by the market. The two markets are not linked, and this is why the European Union is proposing a price cap only on Russian gas.

First, the concept of the double dissolution. Some people who have spoken in the House have confused a double dissolution with the concept of a hung parliament. It is the concept of a hung parliament that they do not understand. A hung parliament is one in which no party or coalition has a majority of seats in the House of Representatives. If no party or coalition can command a majority in the House of Representatives, a new government cannot be formed. In the event that a new government cannot be formed, the Governor-General has a range of powers in which he or she can decide how to proceed. He or she may invite the leader of the largest party or coalition to form a new government or he or she may dissolve both houses of the parliament. The reason the Governor-General has these powers is because of the Constitution of Australia and the British system of government that we have inherited and which we are now trying to change. In the event that the Governor-General dissolves both houses of the parliament, a double dissolution election is held. This is a double dissolution, not a hung parliament.
I understand that many people are under the impression that there is a hung parliament in this House. That is not the case. The government has 76 seats. The opposition has 69. There are three independents and five crossbenchers, including my colleague in this place, Bob Katter. There is a majority government and there is no hung parliament. There is a double dissolution because the government was denied the right to pass legislation in the Senate and the Senate was obstructing the normal processes of government.

I was a Conservative Whip, and it is a privilege to serve on this Bill because it deals with one of the most important issues of our time. We are talking about the protection of the environment and natural resources, which are fundamental to the UK’s future prosperity. If the Bill is successful, it will set the standard for the world for the protection of the environment.
It is very important to protect the natural environment, which is fundamental to the prosperity of the country and to the lives of people around the world, but we must also protect the interests of the people who live in this country today and in future generations, and this is the fundamental basis of this Bill.
The Bill is a very important one. It is a landmark Bill because, after 50 years, the Government are setting out a plan for the future. The Bill is, in effect, a new constitution, in that it is setting out the future of the way in which we manage the environment. There are two objectives in the Bill. The first is to protect and enhance the natural environment, and the second is to improve the quality of life for current and future generations. I am sure that that will be welcomed across the House.
It is clear that we cannot manage the environment without a proper system of governance. The Bill will be the first piece of legislation to establish a new regulatory and accountability framework for the environment. It will replace the current patchwork of environmental laws with a single, cohesive, clear, accountable and coherent regulatory regime.
The Bill will be the foundation of a new system of governance for the environment, ensuring that the Government are held to account for their environmental objectives. It will also ensure that the UK is able to work with its European partners to meet its international obligations.

My view is that the Stability and Growth Pact, which aims to ensure fiscal discipline and prevent excessive deficits, has been largely ineffective in addressing the current economic challenges. While it is true that many countries are facing deficits well above the 3% threshold set by the pact, the reality is that the pact's rules are too rigid and fail to account for the diverse economic conditions across member states. The escape clause, which allows for derogations from the deficit rules during exceptional circumstances, has indeed been triggered, reflecting the unprecedented nature of the current crisis. 

However, the pact's primary issue lies in its inability to provide flexibility for countries with different economic structures and needs. For instance, countries with high unemployment rates or those heavily reliant on social spending may require more lenient fiscal policies to support recovery. The pact's focus on short-term fiscal targets often overlooks the long-term structural issues that contribute to deficits, such as aging populations, healthcare costs, and infrastructure investment.

Moreover, the pact has not adequately addressed the structural weaknesses in the eurozone, such as the lack of a coordinated fiscal policy and the absence of a banking union. These factors have exacerbated the economic imbalances within the eurozone and made it more difficult for countries to adhere to the pact's rules. As a result, the pact has become a symbol of the eurozone's broader governance challenges, and its effectiveness has been called into question.

In light of these issues, I believe that the pact needs to be reformed to better reflect the diverse economic realities of member states and to provide more flexibility in times of crisis. A more adaptable framework would allow countries to pursue fiscal policies that are tailored to their specific needs, while still maintaining a commitment to long-term sustainability. They have all the advantages of a fixed price contract for the CEO, and all of the disadvantages of a stock option for the shareholders. You think that the CEO who sells off half the company’s assets for cash and a bunch of stock options is going to care much about the long-term value of those stock options? No, he’s not. He’ll walk away from the deal with a huge payoff, and the shareholders will be stuck with a bunch of worthless stock options.
So why don’t we just mandate that CEOs take a fixed price contract? Why do we let them play fast and loose with the shareholders’ money? Because CEOs have so much power, and they’re so good at getting what they want. They say that they need the flexibility to make tough decisions quickly, and that stock options are the only way to make them stick around. And who are we to argue? We’re just shareholders, after all. But I say it’s time to put a stop to this nonsense. CEOs should be held accountable for their actions, just like everyone else.

How many people died of COVID in the UK 2021?
In 2021, there were a total of 143,650 deaths in the United Kingdom, with 132,463 of these deaths occurring in England. This is a 6.3 percent increase compared to the total number of deaths in 2020.
How much did COVID cost the NHS in the UK?
In an article published in the BMJ, the researchers found that the direct cost of COVID-19 to the NHS was £13.6 billion in 2020 and £14.1 billion in 2021, but the indirect cost of care delayed, deferred, or cancelled was estimated at £36 billion in 2020 and £45.6 billion in 2021.
What is the recovery rate of coronavirus?
According to the World Health Organization, COVID-19 has an overall fatality rate of approximately 2%, but this varies widely between countries; for example, the fatality rate in the United States is approximately 3%, whereas the fatality rate in South Korea is 0.7%.

a fee, for example, items that are not recyclable. If the plastic waste is shipped from one country to another, it is typically done under the guise of recyclable plastic, so that it is free to ship. And this is how plastics enter the supply chain of other countries. It is then processed in these countries, and the waste ends up in landfills.
It is also not unusual for plastics to be shipped from one country to another through a third-party broker, who mislabels the plastic waste as recyclable. The plastic waste is then sold to a recycling company in the destination country, which, in turn, ends up with the plastic waste.
What do we mean by 'mislabelled' plastic? It means that the waste is not recyclable, but is labelled as such. It also means that the waste is contaminated with other materials, such as food waste, which makes it unrecyclable.
What is the impact of this mislabelling? It leads to an increase in the amount of plastic waste that is not recycled, but ends up in landfills. This, in turn, leads to an increase in the amount of plastic waste that is shipped to other countries, and this is how plastic waste ends up in the oceans.
What is the solution to this problem? The solution is simple: stop mislabelling plastic waste. This will lead to a decrease in the amount of plastic waste that is shipped to other countries, and a decrease in the amount of plastic waste that ends up in landfills.
The best way to do this is to introduce a ban on the import of plastic waste. This will lead to a decrease in the amount of plastic waste that is shipped to other countries, and a decrease in the amount of plastic waste that ends up in landfills. It will also lead to an increase in the amount of plastic waste that is recycled, which will lead to a decrease in the amount of plastic waste that ends up in the oceans.

The hormone revolution has been one of the greatest medical advances in recent decades. The introduction of the contraceptive pill, followed by hormone replacement therapy, has revolutionized women's health and has been a great boon to many. But this has also been a time of great confusion. Hormones have been both vilified and misunderstood. They have been given a bad press, with many blaming them for all manner of ills, and yet they are the cornerstone of good health.
Hormones are essential to our well-being. They are the chemical messengers of the body, and they regulate how our bodies work. They are what make us tick. Without them, we would not be able to digest food, eliminate toxins, feel happy, or even get up and move around in the morning. They are the reason we get up in the morning and are the driving force behind all our bodily functions.
The more we know about hormones, the more we realize that it is not simply the quantity of hormones that is important, but also the quality. Our bodies are capable of producing only a certain quantity of hormones, but when we introduce an external source of hormones, such as hormone replacement therapy, we are potentially introducing a number of foreign chemicals into our bodies. This can have an impact on our health, and it is important to be aware of this when considering hormone replacement therapy.
It is important to note that not all hormone replacement therapies are the same. There are many different types of hormones available, and each has its own benefits and drawbacks. For example, synthetic hormones, such as those found in the contraceptive pill, are designed to mimic the hormones naturally produced by the body. However, they may not be as effective as natural hormones and can have side effects.
Natural hormone replacement therapies, such as those derived from plants, are generally considered to be safer and more effective than synthetic hormones.

In the first place, I want to address the question of the European Court of Justice. As you know, Mr. Batten, there are two aspects to this. First, the extent to which the Court's jurisdiction extends, and secondly, the extent to which national courts are involved in interpreting and applying Community law. The Government's position is that the Court's jurisdiction should be limited to cases involving the Community institutions and to cases that affect the operation of the internal market. We do not want to see the Court's jurisdiction extended to cases in which national governments act in the exercise of their national powers. National governments and national courts should be free to interpret and apply the law as they see fit, so long as they are not acting in a way that is inconsistent with the Treaties. That is why we have included an amendment to the treaty to cover this.

The Government is also looking at how to improve accessibility for disabled and elderly citizens in Ireland. The task force has a target date of 2016 to complete its work.

The Bill marks an important stage in the further development of our national policy of energy conservation. It is a policy which was first announced in 1974, when the Government stated that the future of our country depended on the extent to which we could conserve our energy resources. The first part of the Act sets out in broad terms the national policy to be followed. I have already said that this is a major step forward in the development of our energy conservation policy. It is a policy which we all accept, and one to which we have been committed for a number of years.
Energy is the most important of all the resources we possess. We are dependent on imported oil for more than half of our total energy needs. We also have to rely on imported gas and coal. These imports are very important for our industry, for our homes, for our transport and for our schools. If we are to continue to use this energy, we must use it efficiently, so that we can rely on it for the future. This Bill makes it clear that the Government have a policy of conserving energy and they intend to use every means available to achieve this policy. The Government are committed to conserving energy, and the Bill makes it clear that the Government will take action to ensure that this policy is implemented.
The Bill sets out the general national policy and then sets out a number of specific provisions which must be implemented to ensure that that policy is achieved.

Sharks are vital to the health of our oceans and our planet. They are apex predators, sitting at the top of the food chain and helping to maintain the balance of the ecosystem. The overfishing of sharks, and the resultant depletion of their numbers, can have catastrophic consequences for the rest of the ecosystem, as we are already beginning to see. The removal of top predators has a "trophic cascade" effect, which means that the whole ecosystem is affected and everything from the population of fish to the amount of carbon that can be stored in the oceans is reduced. Sharks help to remove sick and diseased fish from the water, preventing the spread of disease and protecting other species in the process.
They also help to keep the population of other fish in check, preventing overfishing and ensuring that the ecosystem remains in balance. In addition, sharks are important for the health of coral reefs, as they help to keep the populations of herbivorous fish in check, which in turn helps to prevent the overgrowth of algae that can smother coral reefs and kill off the delicate ecosystem they support.
Sharks have a critical role to play in maintaining the health of our oceans and our planet. If we want to protect the biodiversity of our planet, then we must do everything we can to protect these magnificent creatures from the threat of extinction.

The Climate Action Plan has been described as the biggest transformation in our society since independence. Can you describe the key elements of the plan? How do you see it impacting the lives of the average Irish person?
The Climate Action Plan is an ambitious programme of action. It is not just about mitigating climate change; it is also about adapting to the climate change that is already happening. The plan addresses all of the sectors of the economy. It is a significant change from the approach that we have taken in the past, where we have focused on a few big projects and policies. This plan covers every aspect of our lives, from the way we heat our homes to the way we travel to work. It will require a significant change in the way we live our lives, but it is essential if we are to meet our climate goals.
I think that the average Irish person will be impacted by this plan in a number of ways. For example, there will be more investment in public transport, which will make it easier and cheaper for people to get around. There will also be more investment in cycling and walking infrastructure, which will make it easier and safer for people to cycle and walk. The plan also includes measures to help people to insulate their homes, which will make them more energy efficient and cheaper to heat. There will also be more investment in renewable energy, which will make electricity cheaper and cleaner.
Overall, I think that the Climate Action Plan will have a positive impact on the lives of the average Irish person. It will make our country cleaner, greener, and more sustainable. It will also create new jobs and investment opportunities.

just 12% of female barristers aged 35 and under compared with 18% of male barristers.
In light of this, we decided that it was high time we addressed the gender pay gap among barristers. We commissioned a research project into the reasons behind the gender pay gap and the attrition rates among female barristers.
The main findings of the research were that:
The gender pay gap for barristers is 10% which is much lower than the overall UK average of 19%. The gap is lower for more junior barristers and higher for more senior ones.
There are many reasons for the gender pay gap among barristers:
The most senior barristers are almost exclusively male and those who are most successful in their practice are also disproportionately male. This may be because women are less likely to seek work and because women are more likely to work part-time.
There is evidence that women are more likely to leave the profession at a younger age than men. Although women may initially have better academic results at university, this is reversed during their time at the BPTC. This may be because the teaching and assessment methods are not suited to women and women may be less able to cope with the pressure of the BPTC.
There is a lack of female role models and mentors for young women.
Our research also revealed that many female barristers are reluctant to discuss the gender pay gap because they feel that they are expected to be paid less and they are unwilling to draw attention to themselves.
Our recommendations for how to address the gender pay gap among barristers are as follows:
We need to encourage more women to join the profession by making the profession more accessible to women from all backgrounds. This can be achieved by removing the requirement for legal training to be undertaken at university and by providing financial support for women from low-income families.
We need to ensure that the profession is more inclusive of women by providing more flexible working arrangements and by providing more female role models and mentors.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) provides funding to pay for successful outcomes. It is a performance-based model whereby the provider is paid only when a participant is successfully employed for a period of 13 weeks.
The model is underpinned by a ‘whole person’ approach. This means that the JobPath provider is paid to address an individual’s needs as a whole, and not just their employment needs. The JobPath approach recognises the multiple barriers that can exist for the long-term unemployed and that the impact of these barriers on an individual’s life cannot be separated.
The DWP funded a study that evaluated the JobPath scheme. The evaluation was conducted in 2010 and 2011. It was carried out by the London School of Economics and the Institute for Employment Studies. The evaluation explored the experiences of JobPath providers, participants and DWP staff, as well as the cost of the JobPath model.
In 2010, 10 JobPath contractors were selected through a competitive tendering process to deliver services to jobseekers across England, Wales and Scotland. The jobseekers were chosen by the DWP based on their experience of being unemployed, and the difficulties they experienced in finding and staying in work. The DWP provided funding to each of the JobPath contractors to pay for successful outcomes. This means that the contractors were paid when the participants completed their 13-week trial period and became employed. In total, 1,675 participants were supported by JobPath.
The study found that JobPath is a model that addresses the multiple barriers that long-term unemployed jobseekers face in finding and keeping a job. It does this by using an intensive and holistic approach to support jobseekers.
JobPath has been successful in helping its participants to find work, particularly for those with the most complex needs and for those who have experienced long-term unemployment.
JobPath is a more cost-effective model of employment

The 2015 Paris agreement was a landmark achievement that united almost 200 countries in the fight to prevent catastrophic climate change.
