Could you provide a breakdown of the different sources of man-made emissions and how they compare to natural emissions in terms of greenhouse gas production?
Certainly. Man-made emissions primarily come from the burning of fossil fuels for energy, transportation, and industrial processes. The largest sources of man-made emissions are from coal-fired power plants, oil and gas extraction, and transportation such as cars and airplanes. Other sources include deforestation, agriculture, and waste disposal.

Natural emissions, on the other hand, come from natural processes such as volcanic eruptions, wildfires, and decomposition of organic matter. While these emissions are part of the natural carbon cycle and have been occurring for millions of years, human activities have greatly increased the amount of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, leading to climate change.

According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), man-made emissions are responsible for about 100% of the increase in greenhouse gases in the atmosphere since the Industrial Revolution. Natural emissions have been relatively stable over the past 10,000 years, and any increase in natural emissions is not significant enough to account for the rapid increase in greenhouse gases we are currently experiencing.

In summary, while natural emissions have always been a part of the Earth's carbon cycle, man-made emissions have greatly increased the amount of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, leading to climate change.

You can check the Ministry for Housing and Urban Development (MHUD) website to see if your property is in a Rent Pressure Zone (RPZ). If it is, you can also check what restrictions apply to it.
What is the current rent pressure zone?
Rental pressure zones are defined as: A zone where median rental increases have been above the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for 3 years. The median annualised CPI increase in New Zealand was 1.9% in the year ended September 2020.
What is rent pressure zones?
A rent pressure zone (RPZ) is a part of the country that has a housing market where rent has risen significantly in the last few years. This is because there is not enough housing to meet demand, so renters have to compete for the properties that are available.
Does rent control increase housing supply?
Rent control leads to a decrease in housing supply. This is because, for example, landlords may have no incentive to build new apartments if they can't charge the market rate. In addition, rent control leads to a reduction in housing quality.

What is your vision for the future of disability services? In 10 years, what would you like to see?
I would like to see a society that works for and supports all members of the community, not just those who are able to live "independent" lives. I would like to see a society that provides supports in the home and in the community for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities that enables them to live in the community and participate in life as a full, valued member. I would like to see a society that doesn't discriminate against people with disabilities.
What does inclusion mean to you?
Inclusion means making sure that every single person in our society is treated with the respect, dignity and compassion that is their human right. Inclusion means that we are working together as a society to create a world in which everyone has access to the resources, supports and services they need to thrive, not just those who happen to be "lucky enough" to be born without disabilities.
What is the most important thing you want to convey to people who do not have a disability?
I would like to convey that a life with a disability is a life worth living. All people deserve to have the opportunity to live their best lives. As a society we have a responsibility to ensure that every person has access to the resources, supports and services they need to live a full, meaningful life. As we have heard, the National Inquiry on Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls was created in response to the report of the Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples in 1996. This report, entitled, “Peace, Honor, and Respect”, stated that the issue of missing and murdered indigenous women and girls was of such importance that it warranted a full-scale investigation. The government of Canada responded to the call for action of the Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples by creating the National Round Table on Aboriginal Women's Issues. The round table was given the mandate to research the causes and impacts of violence against indigenous women and girls and to develop recommendations to help prevent such violence. Over the course of 10 years, the round table met eight times. It had the participation of government representatives, indigenous peoples' organizations, non-governmental organizations, and academics. The round table's work resulted in the publication of two reports in 2005 and 2007. The round table stated that the lack of data and research, the lack of awareness of the scope of the problem, and the lack of comprehensive services were the main causes of violence against indigenous women and girls.
The round table also developed a national action plan to help reduce the incidents of violence against indigenous women and girls. The action plan includes more than 200 recommendations and was sent to federal, provincial, and territorial governments, as well as indigenous organizations. A veteran of World War I, John McCrae wrote a poem that Canadians have come to cherish on Remembrance Day. He saw friends he loved die in the trenches of the First World War. It is a poem that is a reminder that we must never take for granted the sacrifices made by our men and women in uniform. The poem is called "In Flanders Fields". It is in reference to the poppies that grew in the battlefields of World War I. The poem has come to be one of the most well known and recognizable poems about the sacrifice made by those who served in the Canadian Forces.
In Flanders Fields the poppies blow Between the crosses, row on row, That mark our place; and in the sky The larks, still bravely singing, fly Scarce heard amid the guns below.
We are the Dead. Short days ago We lived, felt dawn, saw sunset glow, Loved and were loved, and now we lie In Flanders Fields.
Take up our quarrel with the foe: To you from failing hands we throw The torch; be yours to hold it high. If ye break faith with us who die We shall not sleep, though poppies grow In Flanders Fields.

The Department of Communications, Climate Action and Environment's draft Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Bill 2020 provides for the extension of the 2030 interim emissions reduction target from 30% to 51% by 2030. The Bill also proposes to extend the carbon budget period from 2017 to 2035. The draft Bill further proposes the establishment of an all-island carbon emissions budget for 2018 to 2025. This all-island carbon emissions budget is designed to drive progress in Northern Ireland to address the impact of climate change. The draft Bill also provides for a 70% reduction in carbon emissions by 2050, in line with the European Union's target. The draft Bill provides for an extension to the carbon budget period for the years 2036 to 2040. This will enable the all-island carbon emissions budget to be extended to a 2018 to 2030 period. The Department of Communications, Climate Action and Environment is currently developing a National Low Carbon Development Plan in line with the requirements of the draft Bill. The draft Bill proposes to establish an independent Climate Action Advisory Council to advise the Government on climate action and low carbon development. The draft Bill proposes to introduce a new statutory basis for the Climate Action Plan which will have to be laid before the Oireachtas every five years and will set out the key actions and policy direction required for the next five years. The draft Bill proposes to establish an annual reporting requirement, with the first report due in October 2020. This report will track progress against the all-island carbon emissions budget. This will be followed by an annual report of progress against the carbon budgets every year after that. The report will be laid before the Oireachtas and will also be laid before the Northern Ireland Assembly.

I would like to provide some examples of other countries and jurisdictions that have implemented measures that are similar to, or even exceed, the policy that we are debating today.
In 2015, the Supreme Court of India ruled that Internet access is a fundamental right under the country's constitution. The Court stated that Internet access is necessary for people to exercise their right to freedom of speech and expression, and for people to participate fully in society. The Court also recognized that many people in rural areas of India do not have access to the Internet, and that this is a violation of their fundamental rights. In response, the Indian government launched the National Digital Literacy Mission, which aims to provide digital literacy training to 50 million people in India by 2020. The government also launched the Digital India initiative, which aims to provide broadband Internet access to all villages in India by 2022. These initiatives are helping to ensure that all Indians have access to the Internet, and that they can participate fully in the digital economy.
In 2018, the Supreme Court of Colombia ruled that Internet access is a fundamental right under the country's constitution. The Court stated that Internet access is necessary for people to exercise their right to freedom of expression, and for people to participate fully in society. The Court also recognized that many people in rural areas of Colombia do not have access to the Internet, and that this is a violation of their fundamental rights. In response, the Colombian government launched the Plan Nacional de Televisión Digital Terrestre, which aims to provide digital television and Internet access to all Colombians by 2020. The government also launched the Programa de Conectividad Rural, which aims to provide broadband Internet access to all rural areas of Colombia by 2022. These initiatives are helping to ensure that all Colombians have access to the Internet, and that they can participate fully in the digital economy.

The bill has been designed to improve educational outcomes for all children and young people. The Education (Scotland) Act 2016 has put in place a robust framework to achieve that. It has given local authorities responsibility for promoting the education and skills of children and young people and a duty to secure the improvement of educational outcomes. It has also given them a responsibility to work with their partners to develop a coherent education strategy, to publish that strategy and to review it annually.
Local authorities must make decisions on the basis of their strategy and must consult with parents, children and young people and with relevant partners. The Scottish Government has committed to publishing a new national education strategy for Scotland in the new year. It will provide a vision for education and set the framework for the work of local authorities to improve outcomes for children and young people.
The education bill provides a new legal framework to enable local authorities to deliver those objectives, to ensure that our children and young people have the best possible start in life. The bill gives local authorities a new duty to work with parents and young people to understand their needs and expectations in relation to education and skills and to help to address any needs that may arise. It will strengthen the role of the local education partnerships, which are made up of the local authority, the head teachers of the schools in their area, parents and other relevant organisations.
The bill will help to support children and young people who have additional support needs, to help them to achieve their potential and to make sure that they have the skills and qualifications that they need to make the transition to work, further education or higher education. To ensure the accuracy of the figures, the government relies on data from reputable sources such as the Central Statistics Office (CSO) and other independent research institutions. These organizations collect and analyze rental data using standardized methods, ensuring that the figures are reliable and comparable over time.

These include increasing the supply of affordable housing, implementing rent control measures in certain areas, and introducing policies to support first-time buyers. Stein, of course, would go on to win three European Cups, but he had a tremendous impact on the club from the very beginning. In 1966, Stein persuaded Billy to play in the final of the Scottish Cup against Hibs and Billy produced one of his finest performances in a 2-1 victory. He played in the Scottish Cup final for the last time in 1967, when Celtic beat Dundee 2-1 to regain the trophy, but a back injury caused him to miss much of the season and his last appearance for the club was a friendly against Aberdeen on 27 May 1968. Billy, along with John Fallon and Jimmy Johnstone, had been signed by Stein, and the three formed a close friendship that would last the rest of their lives. Billy retired from playing in 1968 but would continue to be involved with Celtic in a managerial and coaching capacity, and in an administrative role, until the end of his life. Billy McKay, who retired in 1968 after a 15-year career at Celtic Park, started his coaching career as manager of Celtic Boys' Club, which included a spell as interim manager during the 1969/70 season. He was appointed assistant to Jock Stein in 1972 and was heavily involved in the club's European Cup win in 1970. He was also manager of the Celtic Youth Team during this time. His role was to manage the players in training and during matches. Following Jock Stein's death in 1985, Billy was appointed interim manager and led the club to the Scottish Cup Final where they were defeated by Aberdeen

I remember the days when there was one pub in every village. I used to love going to the pub and meeting people. I would always buy a drink for my friends. The pub was the place where we could meet and mingle.
It was also where we would get together and have a chat, whether it was the local people or someone who had just come to town. We could talk about football, politics, or our jobs. You would get an earful about your boss, or how you were going to be sacked. It was the only place where people could get together and let off steam.
You didn’t have to be rich to go to the pub. You could go in, have a chat with your friends and get a pint for 50p. The pub was also a place where you could go and meet someone new. I remember meeting my wife in a pub. I had gone there with a friend and we were looking for someone to go home with. We spotted two young ladies who had just arrived, and we went over to them and introduced ourselves. The rest, as they say, is history.
The pub was also a place where you could go and watch the football. I remember going to a local pub to watch a game. We all sat there and watched it on a big screen. The atmosphere was electric. When your team scored, everyone would jump up and cheer. When they didn’t score, everyone would sit there in silence.
The pub was also a place where you could go and listen to live music. I remember going to a local pub to see a band. The atmosphere was great. Everyone was dancing and singing along to the music. It was a real party.
The pub was also a place where you could go and play darts. I remember going to a local pub to play darts.

The argument that the motion’s impact on Northern Ireland is minimal is invalid. The motion would remove all of the devolved powers of the Northern Ireland assembly and executive to legislate on abortion. It would also remove the right of the Northern Ireland courts to hear cases on abortion, so that all cases would have to go to the courts in England and Wales. In doing so, it would overturn the abortion law that was passed in 1967, which has served the people of England and Wales for more than 50 years. The motion is not about abortion, and it is not about women’s rights—it is about changing the law.

When a person is released under the parole order they are not out of prison; they are still subject to imprisonment. If they break a condition, they can be recalled to prison and held for the remainder of the sentence. They are not released from imprisonment.

If we go back to the original example, in which a person was released on parole and then re-arrested a month later, and then the parole was revoked, the parole order is revoked as of the date of the original parole order. The GNECB was established in 2009 as the primary agency responsible for investigating complex economic crime in Ireland, particularly those cases which involve criminal activity that may also be prosecuted as money laundering. The GNECB was established in response to the growing concern about the increase in economic crime, particularly corporate crime and fraud, and the need to provide a national co-ordinated response to the problem. The GNECB is the only unit in the State dedicated to investigating economic crime, and is a specialised unit within the Garda.
The GNECB's first priority is to undertake investigations into suspected money laundering. The GNECB undertakes investigations into other types of economic crime including serious fraud, corporate fraud, tax offences, bribery and corruption and other related offences. The GNECB has developed an extensive network of contacts with other domestic and international agencies and is recognised internationally as a specialist unit in its field.
The GNECB is funded by the State and is a dedicated unit within the Garda. It is not a body established under a statutory regime, such as the Commission for Aviation Regulation, the Broadcasting Authority of Ireland or the Competition Authority, which are each established under specific legislation. The GNECB has not been established under any statute. The GNECB is not funded by any other source but the State. The GNECB is under the direct operational control of An Garda Síochána. The Amish people in the United States and Canada have their roots in the Swiss Brethren and Mennonites of the 16th century Anabaptist movement. The term “Amish” is not a reference to a particular church, but rather a denomination of people. Amish people are very religious and practice a faith that traces its roots back to the radical reform movement in 16th century Europe. They are religiously devout and live out their beliefs by strictly adhering to the Bible and rejecting all forms of technology that they believe detract from a simpler life and a closer relationship with God. The Amish are not against technology itself but are against the consumerism and materialism that comes with it. The Amish believe that it is the world’s way that is wrong and not technology itself. That being said, they are not opposed to technology when it comes to farming or business.
They believe that if God wants them to use a certain technology, he will make it available to them. If God does not want them to use a certain technology, then they will not use it. The Amish believe that it is their duty to separate themselves from the world and its values. They believe that the world is too corrupt and that they must remain pure in order to be worthy of God’s grace. The media tend to focus on the criminal aspects of cowboy building – the dodgy builders who refuse to repair faults, or do not have the requisite insurance. It is not surprising that they do so because the criminal side of things can be shocking. I’ve read stories about unlicensed builders who have been involved in the deaths of innocent people, and the number of stories like this is too high.
So how do we combat these cowboy builders? The answer is simple: by raising the standards of building across the board, and the only way to do that is by increasing the number of properly trained and licensed professionals in the industry. This is why the establishment of a national body is so important.
The National Professional Builder Council will do this in a number of ways. The most obvious way is by raising standards through setting a minimum competency threshold for entry. There is a clear gap in the market for this – we need to set standards, and then enforce them.
The other thing that we need to do is to create a body that can represent all the players in the industry – not just developers, builders, or architects, but also plumbers, electricians, and others. The current industry is fragmented, and there needs to be a more holistic approach to the whole industry.
The council’s goal is to create a more level playing field for all those involved in the industry – to make it easier to find a quality builder, or developer, or architect, and to create a system where those involved in the industry can all work together to improve standards.
The creation of the National Professional Builder Council is a necessary step in this process. We need to ensure that the construction industry is fit for purpose, and that it can deliver the housing and infrastructure that Australia needs. This is not just about economic growth – it is about the wellbeing of all Australians, and their ability to live in safe and affordable homes.
